citation.title: Field Experimental Designs for the Study of Media Effects

standing_assumptions:
The article (Political Communication 31:168–180, 2014; PDF pp. 2–14, PDF p. 1 being the publisher's cover page) is an overview of experimental designs. It has no theorem, no displayed formula, no mathematical notation, no table or figure and no formal model; every statistical claim is made in words. The setting those claims inherit, as printed (read from the page images):
[Basic design and its assumptions: section ‘Between-Subjects Design’, p. 170 (PDF p. 4)] “The most basic experimental design is one in which subjects are assigned individually and with identical probability to treatment or control conditions. Assuming that (a) the random assignments are implemented as planned and outcomes are observed for all subjects, (b) the only systematic factor that causes the treatment group to differ from the control group is the intended treatment, and (c) subjects respond solely to the treatment that they receive (and are unaffected by treatments administered to others), the between-subjects design provides the basis for unbiased estimation of the average causal effect of the treatment in the subject pool (Gerber & Green, 2012). Indeed, the estimation of the average causal effect is simple and intuitive: The average outcome in the control group is subtracted from the average outcome in the treatment group.”
[Clustered design: section ‘Between-Subjects Clustered Design’, p. 171 (PDF p. 5)] “Accordingly, researchers studying the effects of TV or radio randomly assign their treatments to geographic clusters. In effect, all individuals living within the same geographic cluster are assigned together to either treatment or control conditions. In the between-subjects clustered design, clusters are assigned independently, but individuals within clusters are not.”
[Estimand under clustering: p. 172 (PDF p. 6)] “The design suggestions given above presuppose that a researcher’s aim in conducting a clustered experiment is the estimation of an \emph{individual-level} average treatment effect.”
[Randomization inference: p. 172 (PDF p. 6)] “One option in such settings is hypothesis testing based on the method of randomization inference (Fisher, 1935; Rosenbaum, 2002). Under the null hypothesis of no treatment effect whatsoever, one may simulate the sampling distribution of possible estimated treatment effects under all possible random assignments. The $p$ value of the observed estimate is calculated based on its location relative to this randomization distribution.”
[No interference: Note 2, p. 177 (PDF p. 11), attached on p. 171 to the discussion of spillovers in Bond et al.] “2. Modeling spillovers in this way in effect relaxes the assumption that subjects are affected solely by their own treatment status and not the status of others.”
Not stated anywhere in the article: potential-outcome notation; a formula for any estimator; an assignment mechanism beyond the words quoted (complete randomization of a fixed number of units and independent assignment with a common probability both fit “assigned individually and with identical probability” and “clusters are assigned independently”); a sequence of populations for the consistency statement, or any bound on outcomes or on cluster sizes; a sampling model. The formal renderings in the targets below are therefore the audit's, taken from the validators' derivations and from the two readers' exact checks, in finite-population potential-outcome notation: units $i = 1, \ldots, N$ with fixed potential outcomes $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$; an assignment $Z \in \{0,1\}^N$ that is the only source of randomness (the article's condition (b)); observed outcome $Y_i = Z_iY_i(1) + (1-Z_i)Y_i(0)$ for every unit (conditions (a) and (c)); average effect $\tau = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i [Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$.
What is and is not a target. Two findings are confirmed errors whose correction changes a mathematical statement: P024-A002 (Moderate; p. 174, the stated necessity of a no-other-change assumption under randomized timing) and P024-E002 (Minor; p. 171, consistency stated without a regularity condition). Each has a counterexample and a corrected statement below. P024-E001 (Moderate) is not a target: it is a misreported statistic from a cited study (p. 171 gives the Bond et al. (2012) effect as approximately 0.7 percentage points where the source reports 0.39), a reporting finding with no mathematical statement to correct, and no claim of the article is derived from the number. The other sixteen error-class findings (P024-E005 to P024-E016, P024-N001, P024-N003, P024-N007, P024-N008) are citation, reference-list, spelling and grammar misprints. Of the nine headline claims, P024-H2, P024-H3 and P024-H5 contain a mathematical statement (unbiasedness; bias and consistency; a weighted-average identity) and are targets; P024-H1, P024-H4, P024-H6, P024-H8 and P024-H9 are framing, qualitative or practical claims; the formal content of P024-H7 (sharp-null randomization tests under a randomized schedule) is part (b) of P024-T2.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Between-Subjects Clustered Design’, second paragraph; audit correction: conditional unbiasedness for positive equal-size clusters and a conditional unequal-size bias witness under an independent Bernoulli parent assignment
canonical_claim.location: p. 171 (PDF p. 5); the estimand is named on p. 172 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement] “Clustered assignment poses two statistical complications. The first is that when clusters contain different numbers of subjects, the standard estimation approach—comparing treatment and control group averages—no longer gives unbiased estimates of the average treatment effect among all subjects (Middleton, 2008, Middleton & Aronow, 2011). The difference-in-means estimator is consistent, which is to say that it converges to the correct answer as the number of clusters becomes very large, but bias may be appreciable in studies with only a few dozen clusters of varying size. In order to mitigate the threat of bias and to improve efficiency, researchers working with clusters of varying sizes may wish to block on cluster size before randomly assigning clusters in each block (Imai, King, & Nall, 2009; Broockman & Green, in press).”
[Corrected formal component: the audit's nonempty-arm conditional reading.] Let $K \ge 2$ clusters have positive integer sizes $n_j$ and arbitrary fixed individual potential outcomes $Y_{ij}(0),Y_{ij}(1)$, under the paper's conditions (a)–(c). The parent assignment treats whole clusters independently with a common probability $p$, $0 < p < 1$: $Z_j \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$. Put $N = \sum_{j=1}^{K} n_j$, $\tau = N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}[Y_{ij}(1)-Y_{ij}(0)]$, and $A = \{0 < \sum_j Z_j < K\}$. Then $\Pr(A)=1-p^K-(1-p)^K>0$. On $A$, define the individual-level difference in means
$$\widehat\tau = \frac{\sum_j Z_j\sum_i Y_{ij}(1)}{\sum_j Z_j n_j} - \frac{\sum_j(1-Z_j)\sum_i Y_{ij}(0)}{\sum_j(1-Z_j)n_j}.$$
(i) [Equal cluster sizes.] If $n_j=n>0$ for every $j$, then $\mathrm E[\widehat\tau\mid A]=\tau$. For each allocation in $A$, with $m=\sum_j Z_j$, the estimator is also $m^{-1}\sum_{j:Z_j=1}\bar Y_j(1)-(K-m)^{-1}\sum_{j:Z_j=0}\bar Y_j(0)$.
(ii) [Unequal cluster sizes; bias is possible.] Take $K=2$, $(n_1,n_2)=(1,2)$ and an independent $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ parent assignment. Set all control outcomes to zero, the small cluster's treatment outcome to zero, and both treatment outcomes in the large cluster to one. Here $\tau=2/3$ and $\Pr(A)=1/2$; conditional on $A$ the two allocations are equiprobable and give $\widehat\tau=0$ and $1$, so $\mathrm E[\widehat\tau\mid A]=1/2\ne 2/3$.
[Scope] These expectations use the normalized conditional law $\Pr(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z\mid A)=\Pr(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z)/\Pr(A)$ for $\mathbf z\in A$. Independence describes the parent assignment, not its conditional law. Arbitrary extensions of the estimator to empty-arm allocations do not affect either conditional conclusion; no unconditional equality for such extensions is asserted. The printed consistency clause and blocking recommendation are not conclusions of this corrected formal component.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The paper assigns whole clusters to treatment or control and says that clusters are assigned independently (p. 171, PDF p. 5); its target is the individual-level average treatment effect (pp. 171–172, PDF pp. 5–6), under conditions (a)–(c) on p. 170. Here $Y_{ij}(z)$ is the fixed potential outcome of individual $i$ in cluster $j$ under cluster assignment $z$; $\bar Y_j(z)=n_j^{-1}\sum_iY_{ij}(z)$. The estimator is the average observed outcome of all treated individuals minus that of all control individuals, defined when both arms contain individuals. The audit's corrected reading specifies an independent common-$p$ Bernoulli parent assignment and then conditions on $A$, the event that both arms are nonempty; conditioning generally induces dependence among cluster assignments. Equal sizes and $K\ge2$ with $0<p<1$ give a positive-probability conditioning event. Neither a potential-outcome formula nor this explicit conditional correction is printed in the paper; these are the audit's formal rendering. The earlier complete-randomization reading in the recorded note is not the assignment law used for these credited conditional components.
canonical_claim.note: The part to formalize here is the first claim (bias when sizes differ), in the audit's formal reading (the paper has no formula). $K$ clusters of sizes $n_j$ with fixed individual potential outcomes; clusters assigned as wholes by complete randomization of $m$ of the $K$ clusters, $1 \le m \le K-1$; estimator $\widehat{\tau}$ as in P024-T4; target the individual average effect $\tau = \sum_j n_j[\bar{Y}_j(1) - \bar{Y}_j(0)]/\sum_j n_j$. (i) [Biased in general when sizes differ; an existence claim.] There are populations with unequal cluster sizes for which $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}] \ne \tau$. Smallest witness, computed when this list was fixed: two clusters of sizes 1 and 2, one treated; $Y(0) = 0$ for all three individuals, $Y(1) = 0$ in the small cluster and $Y(1) = 1$ for both individuals of the large one; $\tau = 2/3$, the two allocations give $\widehat{\tau} = 0$ and $\widehat{\tau} = 1$, and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}] = 1/2$. The Opus reader's witness (runs/P024/fresh-opus/scripts/checks.py, part 2): sizes $(1,1,2,6)$, cluster means of $Y(0)$ equal to $(1,2,3,6)$, constant within-cluster effects $(0,0,1,2)$, two of the four clusters treated; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}] = 547/504$ against $\tau = 7/5$. (ii) [Unbiased when sizes are equal.] If $n_j = n$ for every $j$, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}] = \tau$. The sentence cannot be read as ‘biased whenever sizes differ’: in P024-T4 (iii) the sizes differ and the estimator is exactly unbiased. The consistency clause of the second sentence is false as printed without a regularity condition (finding P024-E002, Minor); it is refuted in P024-T4 and corrected in P024-T5 and is not to be attempted here. ‘Bias may be appreciable in studies with only a few dozen clusters’ is a qualitative remark. The third sentence is a recommendation. Its exact content, as both readers checked it, is (iii) [blocking on size; optional]: if the clusters are partitioned into blocks of equal-sized clusters and the same fraction of the clusters is treated by complete randomization within every block, then $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}] = \tau$ for the pooled difference in means. Opus's instance: sizes $(1,1,6,6)$ with the same outcome pattern, one cluster of each size treated, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}] = \tau = 9/7$, against $31/28$ when two of the four clusters are drawn without blocking. The instances in (i) and (iii) were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Restricted Random Assignment’, first paragraph, with Note 4 (unnumbered statement that under a blocked design the overall estimate is a weighted average of the estimates for each block)
canonical_claim.location: p. 173 (PDF p. 7); Note 4 on p. 177 (PDF p. 11)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 173 (PDF p. 7)] “In order to accommodate the campaign, Gerber et al. (2011) excluded the two largest markets from the random assignment and blocked the remaining markets so that a certain degree of geographic and political balance was ensured. The first restriction effectively limited the broadcast TV experiment to the 18 smaller markets. The second restriction meant that data had to be analyzed in a manner that took the blocked design into account; in effect, the overall estimate of the average causal effect represents a weighted average of the estimate for each block.$^{4}$”
[Note 4, p. 177 (PDF p. 11)] “4. For a step-by-step explanation of the inverse-probability-weighted (Horvitz & Thompson, 1952) estimation of average causal effects under a blocked design or restricted random assignment, see Gerber and Green (2012, chapters 3 and 4, with technical details in Aronow & Middleton, 2013).”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The paper defines a block-randomized experiment on pp. 170–171 (PDF pp. 4–5): “the block-randomized experiment, wherein researchers randomize within predetermined blocks in order to improve efficiency.” It does not define ‘the estimate for each block’, the weights of the weighted average or the inverse-probability-weighted estimator; Note 4 names the estimator (Horvitz & Thompson, 1952) and refers to Gerber and Green (2012, chapters 3 and 4) and Aronow and Middleton (2013), which are not staged. Standard meanings, as used by both readers: the estimate for block $b$ is the difference in means within the block; the weights are the block shares $N_b/N$ of the randomized units; the inverse-probability-weighted estimator is $\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\left[\frac{Z_iY_i}{\pi_i} - \frac{(1-Z_i)Y_i}{1-\pi_i}\right]$ with $\pi_i$ the unit's probability of assignment to treatment.
canonical_claim.note: A verbal statement of an identity. The estimator and the weights are not printed, so the rendering below is the audit's (from the estimator Note 4 names and the two readers' checks), and a fidelity check should treat it as a reading and not as the paper's formula. Formal reading: the randomized units (in the example the 18 media markets; the two excluded markets are outside the randomization and the estimand) are partitioned into blocks $b = 1, \ldots, B$ with $N_b$ units, $N = \sum_b N_b$; within block $b$ the treated set is uniform over the subsets of size $m_b$, $1 \le m_b \le N_b - 1$; $\pi_b = m_b/N_b$; potential outcomes are fixed and $Y_i = Y_i(Z_i)$ is observed for every unit. (i) [Identity, on every allocation] $$\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\left[\frac{Z_iY_i}{\pi_{b(i)}} - \frac{(1-Z_i)Y_i}{1-\pi_{b(i)}}\right] = \sum_b \frac{N_b}{N}\left(\bar{Y}^{T}_b - \bar{Y}^{C}_b\right),$$ where $\bar{Y}^{T}_b$ and $\bar{Y}^{C}_b$ are the treated and control means in block $b$ and $b(i)$ is the block of unit $i$. (ii) [Unbiasedness] the expectation of either side is $\tau = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$. Independence of the assignments across blocks is not needed for (i) or (ii). (iii) [Why the blocks must be taken into account; optional] when the $\pi_b$ differ, the pooled difference in means can be biased. Opus's witness (runs/P024/fresh-opus/scripts/checks.py, part 4): two blocks of four units; block A with $Y(0) = (1,2,3,2)$, $Y(1) = (2,3,4,3)$ and one unit treated; block B with $Y(0) = (10,12,11,13)$, $Y(1) = (15,17,16,18)$ and three units treated. Then $\tau = 3$, the pooled difference in means has expectation $35/4$, and the block-weighted estimator equals the inverse-probability-weighted estimator on each of the 16 allocations and has expectation 3 (recomputed exactly when this list was fixed). Both readers report that the statement held up (Sol with the caveat that the cited campaign's actual assignment and analysis cannot be reproduced from the overview), and no confirmed finding touches it (P024-N005, on the rollout counts of the same example, was not confirmed). In the Texas example the units are media markets whose outcomes are tracked over several weeks; the reading above is at the level of the randomized units with one outcome each, which is all the sentence asserts.
